senses: the greatest of the Roman orators and writers
la:noun:Cicero.html:
Cĭcĕro, ōnis, m., = Κικέρων,
a Roman cognomen in the gens Tullia.
M. Tullius Cicero, the greatest of the Roman orators and writers; born on the 3d of January, 106 B.C. (648 A.U.C.), at Arpinum (hence Arpinae chartae, ); assassinated, at the age of sixty-three years, by the soldiers of Antonius, 43 B.C. (711 A.U.C.): ille se profecisse sciat, cui Cicero valde placebit,; — Hence,
Cĭcĕrōnĭānus, a, um, adj., Ciceronian: simplicitas, Plin. praef. § 22: mensa,: aquae,in the villa of Cicero, at Puteoli, medicinal to the eyes,.—Subst.: Ciceronianus es, non Christianus,i. e. a follower of Cicero,, n. 30.—
Q. Tullius Cicero, the brother of I., whose work, De petitione consulatūs, is yet extant.

la:noun:cicuta.html:
cĭcūta, ae, f.,
the hemlock given to criminals as poison; prob. either Cicuta virosa or Conium maculatum, Linn.; ; ; ; ; plur., ; drunk by Socrates; hence: magister sorbitio tollit quem dira cicutae,i. e. Socrates,—To the extraordinary coldness produced by it, reference is made in .—
Meton., a pipe or flute made from the stalks of the hemlock, a shepherd's pipe, ; ; ; .

la:noun:ciconia.html:
cĭcōnĭa, ae, f.,
a stork, ; ; ; ; at Praeneste called conia, .—
Meton.
A derisory bending of the fingers in the form of a stork's bill, ; Hier. prol. in Sophon. Ep. 125, n. 18.—
An implement in the form of a T, used by rustics to measure the depth of furrows, .—
A transverse pole, moving upon a perpendicular post, for drawing water, etc. (syn. tolleno), .
